title: Nvidia NVDA Stock Falls 4.4% to $212.21 as AI Financing Fears Hit Chips - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) dropped 4.40% on Thursday and closed at $212.21. In early trading today, U.S. futures pointed lower after the Nasdaq fell around 2.6% in the same session. Nvidia underperformed the index by 1.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI spending can continue at its recent pace and how companies will finance it. Yesterday, the market remained under pressure mainly due to concerns about AI spending and financing costs. Meta shares fell about 7% after its quarterly report, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 6.72%. AMD lost 8.1%. Nvidia’s fall came as investors reassessed the cost of expanding AI infrastructure and the ability of companies to sustain their spending. In an interview with CNBC, Jensen Huang said neocloud demand is “off the charts,” but the capital needed to fund AI infrastructure is scarce. His comments added to concerns that smaller AI companies could struggle to finance expansion, which could slow future orders for Nvidia’s chips. On October 21, Nvidia announced a capacity expansion with six partners including Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL, and Unimicron. The plan aims to lift substrate capacity 2.5x over the next three years and SPIL’s optical-engine capacity about 15x by mid-2027. It shows suppliers are preparing for more demand, but actual orders will depend on how much AI infrastructure companies build. At GTC Berlin, Huang urged Europe to build more AI data centers. In June, Nvidia also entered a $10 Billion initiative with Kazakhstan aiming to build a 100,000-GPU cluster. This adds more demand for AI infrastructure outside the U.S. Nvidia reported $96.2 Billion in fiscal Q2 revenue, up 106% from a year earlier. Data center sales accounted for $89 Billion of the total. For the next quarter, the company expects revenue of $108 Billion, plus or minus 2%, assuming no data center compute revenue from China. According to CFO Colette Kress, fiscal 2028 revenue could grow about 70%. However, rising memory costs are weighing on margins, with Q3 gross margin guided at about 74%. Nvidia’s board has also authorized an additional $150 Billion in share buybacks, bringing the total remaining authorization to $235 Billion. Wall Street is still bullish on Nvidia. Cantor Fitzgerald reiterated its Overweight rating with a $350 price target and named Nvidia a top pick. On the technical front, first and second support sit in the $208 to $210 range. Any break below this range could bring the $200 level into focus. On the upside, first resistance starts at $218.88, followed by the second resistance at $221.97 level. The next major resistance for bulls is $243.37. Nvidia hasn’t confirmed its next earnings date yet. Until then, AI financing concerns and spending updates from major cloud providers could drive NVDA stock. title: Seaport Research Issues Stark Nvidia Warning on Nvidia Stock - TradingView
content: Nvidia NVDA faces mounting competitive pressure and potential financial risks from its growing investment commitments, according to Seaport Research, which maintained its Sell rating on the chipmaker and a $180 price target. Analyst Jay Goldberg said Nvidia's financing arrangements may reflect rising pressure from rivals. He also questioned whether the company's efforts to support customers and secure supplies could create competing demands on its financial resources. Nvidia added roughly $250 billion in commitments during its latest quarter, according to Goldberg. Those obligations include spending to secure components and support data center construction, tying the company more closely to the expansion of AI infrastructure. Goldberg also highlighted a separate financing initiative involving Nvidia, six private equity firms and banks. The proposed platform could provide about $500 billion in funding, with the possibility of reaching $1 trillion. Nvidia would not bear the entire obligation, but the analyst views its role as central to the arrangement. The concern is that financing structures built to accelerate growth could magnify losses if demand for computing capacity weakens. Goldberg warned that infrastructure providers reliant on Nvidia's support could face pressure during a downturn, potentially adding strain when the chipmaker's own sales and cash flow soften. title: Nvidia Stocks Put AI-Factory Downtime in Minerva's Crosshairs - TradingView
content: AI-accelerator leader Nvidia NVDA traded at $212.16, at 9:55 a.m. ET after unveiling Minerva, software aimed at keeping sprawling AI data centers productive. The pitch is straightforward: expensive chips need to keep working. Catching a struggling component early could help operators avoid interruptions that leave valuable computing capacity idle. According to Nvidia's announcement, IREN already uses Minerva, while IBM, Lambda and Tesla plan deployments. Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro also intend to offer the platform to customers. Minerva connects equipment data with running workloads, helping teams investigate bottlenecks, combine related alerts and anticipate failures. That gives Nvidia another foothold in the daily operation of the infrastructure its chips power. The Next Web reported that Nvidia disclosed no Minerva pricing, leaving its revenue potential unclear. The valuation picture adds a useful distinction: a GF Score of 96/100 shows broad fundamental strength, while the weaker GF Value reading suggests valuation deserves closer scrutiny. title: Nvidia's Latest AI Power Play Could Shake Up Video Industry - TradingView
content: Nvidia NVDA and growth investor TCV have backed AI video startup Higgsfield in a new funding extension as the company's user base surpassed 40 million and annual revenue approached $1 billion. The financing extends Higgsfield's August Series B round, which raised $400 million at a $5.4 billion valuation led by DST Global. The company has added roughly 10 million users since its summer funding round, highlighting the pace at which demand for AI-generated video tools is growing. Founded in 2023 by former Snap executive Alex Mashrabov and Kazakhstani AI engineer Yerzat Dulat, Higgsfield combines its own AI engine with about 35 external AI video models. The platform is aimed at brands and creators and supports tools for storyboarding, character creation, audio and final video editing. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang highlighted Higgsfield during a visit to Astana, Kazakhstan, where much of the startup's engineering team is based. Huang said AI video systems have improved dramatically, particularly in their ability to create longer videos while maintaining consistency across characters and scenes. He attributed much of that improvement to advances in agentic reasoning systems. The funding also comes as competition across AI video heats up. China's Kling AI reportedly raised $2.8 billion at a $15 billion valuation this summer, while U.S. rival Runway AI raised $315 million at a $5.3 billion valuation earlier this year in a round that also included Nvidia. I think the most important takeaway is that AI video is moving very quickly from experimentation toward a real commercial market. Higgsfield's combination of 40 million users and a revenue run rate nearing $1 billion suggests creators and enterprises are already willing to pay for these tools at scale. For Nvidia, the strategic logic is straightforward. More sophisticated video generation means more inference and training demand, which ultimately supports demand for GPUs and AI infrastructure. The bigger question is how durable the economics will be. Video generation remains compute-intensive, and the sector is attracting enormous amounts of capital from both U.S. and Chinese competitors. For investors, the key things to watch are Higgsfield's revenue growth, user monetization, compute costs, competitive differentiation and whether AI video usage continues expanding beyond creators into enterprise workflows. title: NVDA vs. LRCX: Which AI Semiconductor Stock Is the Better Buy? - The Globe and Mail

Both companies are benefiting from rising AI infrastructure investments, but their growth opportunities, valuations and risks differ. With NVIDIA trading at a lower price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple and Lam Research delivering stronger year-to-date stock gains, which semiconductor stock offers investors a better buying opportunity today? Let’s find out. NVIDIA delivered an impressive second-quarter fiscal 2027 performance, with revenues soaring 106% year over year to $96.22 billion. Geopolitical uncertainty also remains a concern, with the company's forward outlook assuming no Data Center compute revenues from China. Despite these risks, NVIDIA's strong profitability, computing ecosystem and expanding customer base support its long-term investment appeal. Lam Research is benefiting from growing semiconductor manufacturing requirements as AI chips, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging become increasingly complex. Nevertheless, Lam Research remains exposed to semiconductor capital-spending cycles. Clean-room availability and component shortages are restricting industry output, and near-term constraints limited its second-quarter revenue guidance to $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million. The revenue guidance reflects a 4.6% sequential increase, significantly lower than the 22.3% increase in the second quarter. China supplied 35% of first-quarter revenues, but management expects a meaningfully lower share in the second quarter. These factors could affect near-term growth. Analysts’ projections suggest NVDA has a better growth profile than LRCX. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NVIDIA’s fiscal 2027 revenues and EPS indicates a year-over-year increase of 88.7% and 95%, respectively. NVIDIA has the valuation advantage, trading at a forward 12-month P/E multiple of 15.18 compared with 23.02 for Lam Research. Lam Research has delivered superior stock market momentum, with shares rising 33.4% year to date compared with a 13.8% gain for NVIDIA. However, NVDA's lower valuation and stronger growth profile make it more attractive than LRCX. Lam Research offers compelling exposure to rising semiconductor manufacturing spending, advanced packaging and memory production. Its record profitability and favorable industry outlook make it a strong contender. However, NVIDIA appears to be the better investment bet today. Its faster growth, 75% gross margin, expanding AI customer base and lower P/E multiple offer a more attractive mix of growth and relative value. Supply constraints, memory costs and geopolitical risks remain important considerations, but NVIDIA's leadership in AI computing gives it the edge. title: Nvidia Earnings Are Coming Next Month and the Stock Looks Poised to Dip Regardless of the Outcome - The Motley Fool
content: You may be surprised at how the market has reacted to most of the chip giant's recent quarters. Earnings season has kicked off, but the world's most valuable company by market cap doesn't report until next month. Nvidia (NVDA -0.59%) operates on a different fiscal calendar, with its fiscal third quarter ending next week. It doesn't mean investors shouldn't start preparing now for the initial market reaction. When the global leader in AI infrastructure solutions offers up fresh financials in mid-November, the numbers will be big. The stock's response -- at least, based on recent market reactions to Nvidia results -- might surprise you. Analysts are holding out for another quarter of robust growth for Nvidia. They see revenue surging 91% to hit a record $109 billion. This is in line with the $108 billion that Nvidia itself offered up as guidance two months ago. The same Wall Street pros also see earnings rising roughly 90%, to $2.47 per share. You would think a 90% increase on both ends of the income statement is a pretty high bar, but Nvidia is often toying with the market. It has consistently landed 3% to 6% above analyst profit targets over the past year. With its recent string of beat-and-raise performances, you would expect confetti launchers to go off whenever the wearer of the market cap crown steps up with new financial results. The last five quarters could shock you. There is a lot to unpack here. Let's start by noting that the stock initially moved lower following four of the last five earnings reports. The good news is that the stock had ultimately risen by the time Nvidia reported again three months later. Another piece of comforting news is that the outlier here -- Nvidia shares rising after its fiscal second quarter this past summer -- was the one time that the stock was lower than it was after the previous report. The conclusion, given the limited sample size of five financial updates, is that Nvidia more than makes up for the initial post-earnings decline. The one time that didn't happen, the initial post-earnings reaction was positive. This brings us to next month's critical update. Nvidia stock is currently near its level from its last report on Aug. 26. It's not trading materially higher, suggesting the stock may sell even on an upbeat report. It's also not trading substantially lower, as it did when it bucked the trend to rise last time out. One comforting thought for the bulls is that the stock has undershot the improvement in Nvidia's fundamentals over the past year. Revenue growth has accelerated over the past several quarters, and net income growth has been explosive. The stock's 20% ascent over the past year is just a sliver of the growth it has delivered. Nvidia shares are currently trading for less than 14 times next year's adjusted earnings target. It's a great price for a great company. The ceiling remains high. Naturally, the floor can also be substantially lower if revenue growth slows and margins contract, but that's not likely to be the case in next month's report. If a dip comes -- as it has four of the last five times -- there are still good reasons to remain optimistic. Rick Munarriz has positions in Nvidia. title: NVDA Logs Best Day In Over A Month: Burry Spotlights Partnership Blitz — Analyst Calls Full-Stack Strategy ‘Underappreciated’ - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) logged their best day in over a month on Wednesday as “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry spotlighted a wave of partnership announcements and analyst Gene Munster argued that investors still underappreciated the company’s full-stack AI strategy. NVDA stock closed nearly 3% higher at $221.97 after a string of announcements at GTC Berlin, before slipping about 1.6% overnight early on Thursday. “Massive Partnership news day for NVDA,” Burry said in a subscriber chat on Cassandra Unchained. Google Cloud plans to launch general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances in November, with European expansion planned. Its infrastructure could eventually scale to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Dell’s AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter. HPE expanded its enterprise AI offerings, while Nutanix and Netris announced infrastructure work for AI cloud providers. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian with Nvidia OpenShell and plans to add Sentry integration on BlueField-4 processors to enforce security policies in hardware. Quantum X Labs reported improved error-correction results using Nvidia’s CUDA-Q software. Nvidia is also in talks about further investment in GPU cloud provider Firmus, The Information reported. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said Nvidia’s integrated platform creates a lasting business advantage. “Software + libraries + hardware form a full stack that raises switching costs and supports recurring upgrade cycles,” he said on X, calling the strategy “Still underappreciated by investors.” CEO Jensen Huang echoed the message: “NVIDIA today is really a full stack, end-to-end, complete AI factory platform.” Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and established more than 12,000 partnerships across the region. Vera Rubin is in full production, he said, claiming 30 times Blackwell’s performance in large language model processing. Nvidia’s factory-assembled DSX Pod integrates computing, networking and cooling. Huang said it could cut the time from equipment arrival to token production from four to five months to about one month. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle CapEx will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable,” he said. Vertiv said its Nvidia DSX-based approach could produce up to 30% more cumulative tokens in the first 12 months from project kickoff under modeled assumptions, using the same installed capacity. Polar Data Centers is applying the approach to a 41-megawatt development phase in Norway. “Agents think, reason, iterate, use tools, and as a result, consume an enormous amount of tokens,” Huang said. “GPU demand has really gone through the roof.” Munster sees the trend sustaining computing demand. “Agents can consume 10-15x the tokens of a chatbot. Today roughly 15m consumers use bots daily. In a few years that could be billions,” he said. Nvidia’s OpenShell controls agents’ access to files, networks and tools, with Sentry adding hardware-based monitoring. “I'm delighted to say that Anthropic and NVIDIA are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents,” Huang said. He also expects software suppliers to become agent providers. Munster was more selective, saying that Salesforce and Adobe could struggle while security and data-monitoring companies benefit from increased activity and complexity. Huang announced Hyperion-compatible vehicles from Volkswagen, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes. Munster estimated that physical AI could eventually contribute a third of Nvidia’s revenue, versus less than 5% today. Still, he cautioned that automakers face substantial development work. “Hyperion helps traditional automakers build autonomy, but it’s not a turnkey solution, they still lack the data and model,” he said. Nvidia also introduced the Agile ONE reference robot with Agile Robots, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and RTX Spark, developed through a four-year Microsoft partnership. Huang said RTX Spark offers one petaflop of computing performance and 128 gigabytes of memory for local AI development. The keynote included no new financial metrics or guidance, Munster noted. Instead, he highlighted SpaceX’s spending plans ahead of Nvidia’s next earnings report. “Last night’s $SPCX December quarter capex guide of $35-40B (street was at $19B) is a positive read-through for what we should hear from Nvidia on the earnings call in about a month,” he said. Shares of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX) are eyeing their best week in nearly three months after a third-quarter (Q3) earnings beat and strong revenue guidance prompted brokerages to raise their targets. But Morningstar warns that investors may be paying for growth that could take decades to justify the stock’s valuation. SPCX stock closed nearly 8% higher at $159.31 on Wednesday after SpaceX beat Q3 expectations, posting earnings of $0.35 a share versus $0.16 expected and revenue of $14.575 billion against a $13 billion forecast. The company projected Q1 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion, Q4 capital spending of $35 billion-$40 billion and Q4 gross margins closer to Q2 levels. Morningstar raised its fair value estimate to $70 from $62, reflecting the potential benefits of Starship reuse and greater confidence in terrestrial data center expansion, partly offset by reassessed long-term AI investment returns. Its target still implies a 56% downside from Tuesday’s closing price. At that price, SpaceX’s $1.95 trillion market cap values its shares at 2.11 times Morningstar’s fair value estimate. “The company's aggressively lofty valuation implies investors will have to wait decades for earnings to grow into SpaceX's multiples,” Morningstar said. The firm acknowledged why Musk’s investors may look beyond near-term financial hurdles. “Loyal holders of companies run by Elon Musk have a very long time horizon and are often willing to look past interim milestones toward the prospects of big bets on moonshot projects and the grander vision on the horizon,” it said. Clear Street raised its target to $248 from $217, implying 56% upside from current levels, and maintained a 'Buy' rating following the stronger-than-expected results and revenue guidance. After increasing near-term forecasts, the brokerage said its estimates “remain conservative beyond 2027, leaving room for upward revisions as new capacity comes online and begins generating revenue.” Meanwhile, Susquehanna lifted its target to $176 from $173, implying 11% upside, while retaining a 'Neutral' rating. It highlighted robust revenue growth and margin expansion as compute leasing deals ramp, but flagged aggressive buildout targets and the dependence of the launch and connectivity businesses on successful Starship commercialization. Morningstar recognizes SpaceX’s competitive strength even as it questions the valuation. “SpaceX has transformed the economics of space launch and dominates the market for lifting spacecraft into orbit, and it has a decade lead on most competitors in experience and payload launch volumes,” it said. SpaceX delivered an estimated 83% of the mass sent into orbit in 2025. Its low internal launch costs also support Starlink’s economics, with Morningstar estimating returns on invested capital in the mid-20% range for the launch and connectivity businesses, above its 9.3% estimated cost of capital. However, uncertainty over heavy AI investment limits SpaceX’s overall moat rating to 'Narrow'. Morningstar expects AI to generate a majority of revenue by the end of 2026. Morningstar forecasts successful reuse of Starship upper stages by late 2028, enabling multiple launches per week and lower launch costs. The stakes extend across satellite connectivity and orbital computing. “If Starship does not prove to be reusable, however, it would put the company’s economic moat and operational future in doubt, as its V3 Starlink satellites and proposed AI satellites don’t fit in Falcon rockets,” it said. Its $70 base case already assumes viable orbital data centers, with 60,000 computing satellites providing 13 gigawatts of capacity and generating $168 billion in annual revenue by 2035. In a more aggressive expansion scenario, annual orbital computing revenue reaches $200 billion, but excessive capital spending and falling rental rates leave SpaceX worth just $26 per share, marking an 84% downside. Morningstar also flagged a potential increase in shares available for public trading. “In the year following SpaceX's IPO of just under 5% of its shares, the remaining 95% will become available for sale by insiders to the public, which could test marginal demand and drive volatility in the stock price,” the firm said. Shares of Lam Research (LRCX) tumbled about 8% to $242 in overnight trading late on Wednesday despite record fiscal first-quarter results, as the chip-equipment maker disclosed supply constraints delaying some shipments and warned that China’s revenue contribution would fall in the December quarter. LRCX stock fell 1% to $260.81 on Wednesday, with shares on pace to log their third straight week of losses after dipping 1% so far this week. Lam reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion, beating the $8.14 billion consensus and setting a fifth consecutive quarterly record. Revenue increased 54% from a year ago and 22% sequentially, while adjusted EPS reached a record $2.20, above the $2.18 estimate. Gross margin improved to 52.4% from 52% in the June quarter. Operating margin climbed to 40.2% from 38.4%, crossing 40% for the first time. Memory systems revenue surged 120% year over year, while NAND revenue grew 40% sequentially. The Customer Support Business Group also delivered strong growth, with revenue rising 40% from a year earlier to nearly $2.5 billion. Lam generated record free cash flow of $3.24 billion and ended the quarter with $7.5 billion in cash and short-term investments, up from $5.6 billion in June. It repurchased $1 billion of shares and paid $325 million in dividends. The company has $3 billion remaining under its overall buyback authorization, with an accelerated repurchase program continuing into December. Its long-term goal remains returning 85% of free cash flow to shareholders. Lam forecast December-quarter revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million, and adjusted EPS of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15, versus consensus of $2.32. Gross and operating margins are expected to reach 52.5% and 40.5%, respectively, each plus or minus one percentage point. However, CFO Doug Bettinger said supply constraints limited the outlook. “I would mention that this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing,” he said. He declined to confirm an analyst’s estimated $300 million to $400 million impact, but said affected December shipments would move into March. CEO Tim Archer said some suppliers face demand growing faster than Lam’s own business. The company is working to expand supplier capacity and would consider investments if needed. “For those of us who were around during the COVID shortages, this is nothing like that. We learned a lot of lessons during that period,” Archer said. “I think we’ll be caught up very shortly.” Lam spent $258 million on capital projects and added about 1,900 employees during Q1. Inventory reached $4.6 billion, while inventory turns improved to a nearly seven-year high. The firm sees longer-term gross margins reaching the mid-50s. However, the adjusted tax rate rose to 16.5% from 11% in June and is expected to remain around that level in December and likely beyond. China accounted for 35% of September revenue, up from 26% in June, but Lam expects the share to fall substantially in December. “I expect that in December we’ll be meaningfully down, driven by the domestic customers in China,” Bettinger said. Multinational customers in China are expected to remain reasonably strong, although Bettinger did not quantify the overall decline. He also expects mature-node spending outside China to strengthen in 2027, with little meaningful growth this year. Lam expects AI demand to sustain semiconductor investment beyond the current supply constraints. “Our preliminary 2027 WFE outlook is for more than $200 billion of spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND,” Archer said. This compares with spending in the mid-$150 billion range expected for 2026. Lam sees demand through 2028 and 10 new major fabs opening in 2027. Foundry logic and DRAM have contributed 80% of systems revenue growth year-to-date. AI’s need for faster storage could further increase equipment demand. “Said differently, for each percentage point mix shift of NAND bits to SLC class devices, approximately 2% more installed wafer capacity will be needed to support the same bit demand,” Archer said. Lam has shipped panel-plating systems to more than 20 customers and secured four backside-power tool-of-record wins at a leading customer. The support business is expected to grow more than 30% in 2026 and more than 15% in 2027, driven by upgrades, spares and services. content: Shares of Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) logged their best day in over a month on Wednesday as “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry spotlighted a wave of partnership announcements and analyst Gene Munster argued that investors still underappreciated the company’s full-stack AI strategy. NVDA stock closed nearly 3% higher at $221.97 after a string of announcements at GTC Berlin, before slipping about 1.6% overnight early on Thursday. “Massive Partnership news day for NVDA,” Burry said in a subscriber chat on Cassandra Unchained. Google Cloud plans to launch general availability of its Vera Rubin-powered A5X instances in November, with European expansion planned. Its infrastructure could eventually scale to 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites. Dell’s AI Factory with Nvidia now serves more than 6,500 customers, up from 5,000 last quarter. HPE expanded its enterprise AI offerings, while Nutanix and Netris announced infrastructure work for AI cloud providers. Meanwhile, CrowdStrike is integrating Falcon Guardian with Nvidia OpenShell and plans to add Sentry integration on BlueField-4 processors to enforce security policies in hardware. Quantum X Labs reported improved error-correction results using Nvidia’s CUDA-Q software. Nvidia is also in talks about further investment in GPU cloud provider Firmus, The Information reported. Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said Nvidia’s integrated platform creates a lasting business advantage. “Software + libraries + hardware form a full stack that raises switching costs and supports recurring upgrade cycles,” he said on X, calling the strategy “Still underappreciated by investors.” CEO Jensen Huang echoed the message: “NVIDIA today is really a full stack, end-to-end, complete AI factory platform.” Huang said Nvidia had invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and established more than 12,000 partnerships across the region. Vera Rubin is in full production, he said, claiming 30 times Blackwell’s performance in large language model processing. Nvidia’s factory-assembled DSX Pod integrates computing, networking and cooling. Huang said it could cut the time from equipment arrival to token production from four to five months to about one month. “The wasted idle compute, the wasted idle CapEx will reduce, and everybody becomes more profitable,” he said. Vertiv said its Nvidia DSX-based approach could produce up to 30% more cumulative tokens in the first 12 months from project kickoff under modeled assumptions, using the same installed capacity. Polar Data Centers is applying the approach to a 41-megawatt development phase in Norway. “Agents think, reason, iterate, use tools, and as a result, consume an enormous amount of tokens,” Huang said. “GPU demand has really gone through the roof.” Munster sees the trend sustaining computing demand. “Agents can consume 10-15x the tokens of a chatbot. Today roughly 15m consumers use bots daily. In a few years that could be billions,” he said. Nvidia’s OpenShell controls agents’ access to files, networks and tools, with Sentry adding hardware-based monitoring. “I'm delighted to say that Anthropic and NVIDIA are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents,” Huang said. He also expects software suppliers to become agent providers. Munster was more selective, saying that Salesforce and Adobe could struggle while security and data-monitoring companies benefit from increased activity and complexity. Huang announced Hyperion-compatible vehicles from Volkswagen, JLR, Volvo and Mercedes. Munster estimated that physical AI could eventually contribute a third of Nvidia’s revenue, versus less than 5% today. Still, he cautioned that automakers face substantial development work. “Hyperion helps traditional automakers build autonomy, but it’s not a turnkey solution, they still lack the data and model,” he said. Nvidia also introduced the Agile ONE reference robot with Agile Robots, expected in the first quarter of 2027, and RTX Spark, developed through a four-year Microsoft partnership. Huang said RTX Spark offers one petaflop of computing performance and 128 gigabytes of memory for local AI development. The keynote included no new financial metrics or guidance, Munster noted. Instead, he highlighted SpaceX’s spending plans ahead of Nvidia’s next earnings report. “Last night’s $SPCX December quarter capex guide of $35-40B (street was at $19B) is a positive read-through for what we should hear from Nvidia on the earnings call in about a month,” he said. title: European Mobility Leaders Build Safe Vehicles and Robotaxi Fleets on NVIDIA Hyperion - NVIDIA Newsroom
content:
GTC Berlin—NVIDIA today announced that leading automakers in Europe and mobility providers, including Bolt with Lucid, Mercedes-Benz, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles and Einride, are showcasing selected autonomous-mobility use cases on the NVIDIA Hyperion computing platform, demonstrating potential applications for level 3 and level 4 vehicles as well as future robotaxi fleets. In addition, Volvo Cars is adopting Hyperion and NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack software for safe automated driving. NVIDIA also introduced new AI and safety technologies to help developers build, validate and deploy autonomous vehicles (AVs) at scale. Autonomous transportation represents a multitrillion-dollar opportunity, with robotaxis leading the move to commercial level 4 deployment. NVIDIA Hyperion and the NVIDIA Halos full-stack safety system give automakers and mobility providers the computing performance, safety foundation and long-term support to bring AVs and robotaxi fleets to market at scale. “Robotaxis are the first mass-market application of robotics and physical AI, reinventing how people and goods move,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “NVIDIA Hyperion, together with our Halos safety operating system, gives our partners a full-stack robotaxi platform designed to achieve full autonomy and the highest levels of safety, bringing us closer to a future where everything that moves is autonomous.” Mobility Leaders in Europe Build on NVIDIA Hyperion
Automakers and mobility providers in Europe are pursuing various paths to autonomy, from passenger vehicles and robotaxi fleets to autonomous freight trucks. NVIDIA Hyperion’s modular architecture supports all of these programs, compatible with NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack autonomous driving software as well as partners’ own driving software. Bolt has selected NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack for its European robotaxi program, beginning with future Lucid vehicles built on Hyperion. Bolt and NVIDIA will adapt the software for European roads and integrate it into vehicles from multiple manufacturers, combining NVIDIA’s driving and safety technologies with Bolt’s fleet-management systems, operations and local market expertise. Bolt plans to begin gathering real-world driving data to support the development and validation of the autonomous driving technology — subject to regulatory approval — in Madrid in 2027, with Germany being a priority for future deployment as part of a planned European rollout of at least 25,000 level 4-capable future Lucid vehicles built on NVIDIA Hyperion. At GTC Berlin, Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is presenting its autonomous ID. Buzz AD vehicle platform with Hyperion to support multiple autonomous-driving systems. Hyperion provides a common computing and sensor architecture designed to simplify integration and validation, helping developers and mobility operators bring robotaxi and commercial transport services to market. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with Hyperion, Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Mercedes-Benz is extending its partnership with NVIDIA on Hyperion and Alpamayo Stack to support the development of the automaker’s L3 and L4 capabilities. The company also announced that MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO, developed in partnership with NVIDIA, will soon get approval for urban point-to-point urban driver assistance in Germany, helping drivers navigate journeys through complex city traffic. Beyond passenger vehicles and robotaxis, Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using Halos, Alpamayo and NVIDIA Cosmos™ open world models to develop and validate its driving system, while TIER IV and the Technical University of Munich plan to integrate Hyperion to develop and validate systems for autonomous public transportation in Germany. NVIDIA technology and manufacturing partners are also helping expand the AV ecosystem, with Aptiv, Valeo and Schaeffler building Hyperion-based computing platforms that can be integrated by vehicle manufacturers for L4 AVs and robotaxis. Scaling Safe Autonomy With NVIDIA Halos
Halos provides the safety foundation for NVIDIA’s AV platform, bringing together AI computing, safety software and validation from development through deployment. To give developers repeatable ways to evaluate driving behavior and simulation accuracy, NVIDIA today introduced Halos SAFE — the Safety Assurance Framework for Evaluation — with dSPACE, IVEX and TÜV Rheinland collaborating on evaluation workflows. Halos SAFE connects simulation, software- and hardware-in-the-loop evaluation, on-road testing and fleet monitoring through defined scenarios, tests and measurable performance criteria to generate traceable safety evidence that supports deployment. The Halos SAFE ecosystem also includes JLR, Mercedes-Benz, Volvo Cars, 51Sim, aiMotive, AVL, Deepen AI, Foretellix and Synopsys. Accelerating AV Development
Developing AVs means teaching AI to handle the diversity of real-world driving, then bringing that intelligence into the vehicle. NVIDIA’s latest models, tools and blueprints help developers prepare driving data, improve models and evaluate performance: Uber and NVIDIA are developing a data factory powered by Cosmos to curate and process data for AV development. The effort is part of a broader partnership spanning AI development infrastructure, Hyperion-based vehicles and Uber’s global ride-hailing network. Porsche is leading the development of a data flywheel workflow across Volkswagen Group brands through Voxel51, using NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory and Omniverse NuRec on Microsoft Azure to turn fleet data into datasets and simulations for evaluating autonomous-driving models. This is expected to reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycle duration by up to 85%. Watch the GTC Berlin keynote from Huang and explore sessions. About NVIDIA
